scenario:
We are moving a rollback-enabled 2D platformer from an old Box2D integration to the current Box2D 3.x C API on Windows and Linux. Our branch mixes 2.4 C++ examples, snippets copied from `main`, and an unrecorded 3.x binary, so the exact API and behavior contract is unclear. Four players share a world with moving and one-way platforms, lifts connected by joints, trigger volumes, fast projectiles, and roughly 2,000 active shapes. The simulation must fit a 3 ms CPU budget while the renderer varies from 48 to 240 Hz.

Today we call `b2World_Step` once per rendered frame with the frame delta and change the substep count when frame time rises. Grounding is a downward ray plus “any contact this frame”; at low frame rates the player flickers between grounded and airborne, lands twice, sticks under one-way platforms, and sometimes slides off a translating platform. The proposed fix is to teleport a dynamic capsule onto the ray hit, disable unwanted contacts after the step, and treat begin/end contact and sensor events as persistent objects. Gameplay retains raw body, shape, and joint IDs indefinitely, destroys them in arbitrary order, and reads those IDs from queued events on later frames. Bullets will be enabled on every moving body because several projectiles tunnel.

For rollback, each machine re-creates the world from spawn records, uses hardware-concurrency as its worker count, replays inputs with the captured render deltas, and compares only the players' final transforms. We assume the same seed makes this deterministic across worker counts, CPUs, compilers, and future 3.x updates. Our performance evidence is one average frame time; we do not yet record step profiles, solver counters, contact/event counts, hash divergence ticks, or a dense-scene/fast-projectile matrix.

Review this design before implementation. First establish a pinned Box2D source/API snapshot and distinguish current 3.x C interfaces from stale 2.4 C++ patterns. Then give a Box2D-specific correction and an executable evidence plan: choose the stepping and substep policy from measured stability/cost rather than an unexplained constant; define body/shape/joint ownership and event/ID lifetimes; resolve sensors, moving platforms, and one-way contacts; choose among a physical body, queries, ray/shape casts, and a custom character controller; scope CCD/bullets; and state what replay determinism can actually be claimed when worker count or build/platform changes. Include the profiling and adversarial tests needed to justify the result, and route generic simulation architecture or rollback work to the appropriate core workflows instead of duplicating them here.

baseline.response:
# Design verdict

Do not implement the proposed fix. It combines a variable simulation clock, post-solve contact changes, transient Box2D data treated as durable state, unconstrained handle lifetimes, blanket CCD, and a replay claim that is much broader than Box2D can support. Those choices explain the observed symptoms and would make rollback failures difficult to localize.

## 1. Establish the Box2D contract first

Make the Box2D revision part of the simulation protocol:

1. Vendor Box2D or use a submodule at one exact tag and commit. Record the commit, source-tree hash, CMake options, compiler and floating-point flags, target architecture, and the hashes of both the installed headers and linked library. Build the Windows and Linux binaries from that source; quarantine the unrecorded binary.
2. Add a small adapter compile/link probe to CI. It should include only the pinned public headers, create and destroy a world/body/shape/joint, install the callbacks actually used, step once, drain each event stream, run each selected query/cast, and read the profile/counters. This catches a header/library mismatch and snippets copied from a later `main`.
3. Record the Box2D version reported by the pinned build, if that revision exposes one, but do not use a semantic version alone as the identity. The commit and binary hash are authoritative.
4. Put every Box2D call behind one adapter. An update to Box2D, solver settings, fixed step, substep count, worker/task configuration, or relevant build flags increments a replay/simulation version and reruns the qualification suite.

The stale 2.4 pattern is a C++ object graph: `b2World`, `b2Body*`, fixtures, `b2Joint*`, a contact-listener class, and `world.Step(dt, velocityIterations, positionIterations)`. The 3.x C interface uses opaque value IDs such as `b2WorldId`, `b2BodyId`, `b2ShapeId`, and `b2JointId`; shapes replace the old fixture-facing usage; operations are free functions; and `b2World_Step(worldId, dt, substepCount)` takes a substep count rather than the 2.4 velocity/position iteration pair. World event getters return per-step buffers, and filtering, pre-solve, task, and query hooks use C callbacks. Exact names, flags, and event fields must come from the pinned headers—never from a 2.4 example or current `main`.

## 2. Make simulation time independent of rendering

Drive Box2D with an integer tick clock and a fixed `dt`. Accumulate render time, execute zero or more fixed ticks, and render an interpolation between the two most recent completed states. A 48 Hz and a 240 Hz renderer must consume the same tick/input stream. Cap catch-up work with an explicit overload policy, but do not enlarge `dt` or change the substep count when rendering is slow. Replay tick numbers and tick inputs, not captured render deltas.

Choose the fixed rate and substep count by a measured matrix, for example fixed rates of 60 and 120 Hz crossed with 1, 2, 4, and 8 substeps. Before running it, define game-unit acceptance limits for maximum penetration, lift/joint drift, grounded-state errors, one-way failures, and projectile misses. Select the cheapest configuration that passes every adversarial scene and the CPU percentile target. Then freeze `dt` and substeps as protocol constants. An average below 3 ms is insufficient: record per-tick p50/p95/p99/max and also the total physics cost of catch-up on a 48 Hz render frame. Leave headroom for event translation and gameplay queries.

## 3. Use a physical character consistently

For this game, start with one dynamic capsule and let Box2D solve its physical contacts. This fits the need to ride translating/rotating platforms, interact with lifts, and receive physical impulses. Drive it with velocity/forces/impulses subject to explicit acceleration limits. Do not teleport it to a ray result; that bypasses continuous collision, injects penetration, destroys meaningful relative velocity, and fights the contact solver.

A downward ray is only a probe. It does not describe the capsule footprint, a usable support normal, or whether the hit is currently touching. Derive support after each fixed step from the capsule's actual contact manifolds (or the pinned revision's body contact-data API): orient the normal toward the character, require a walkable upward normal and relevant contact point/separation, reject sensors, side walls, and ceilings, and identify the supporting body. Maintain a small, explicit support hysteresis/coyote-time policy in ticks if the game wants it. Emit `landed` only on the gameplay transition from unsupported to supported, not once per contact-begin event.

Make moving platforms kinematic and move them on the fixed tick with velocity, or with the pinned API's target-transform facility if present. Do not teleport them per render frame. Continuous kinematic velocity lets the solver's relative velocity and friction carry the capsule. Test friction, acceleration, reversal, rotation, edges, and sleep/wake. If design requires stickier platform behavior than friction provides, implement a bounded gameplay rule using the support body's velocity; do not snap world position.

Queries, rays, and shape casts remain useful for look-ahead, ledge/step tests, spawn validation, and fast swept gameplay tests, but they are not a second collision solver. Prefer a capsule/shape cast over a center ray where the capsule volume matters.

If later acceptance tests show the physical capsule cannot deliver the desired crisp movement, replace it with a custom geometric controller rather than mixing teleportation with a dynamic body. Such a controller should overlap/depenetrate, sweep the capsule, clip/slide against collision planes, apply an explicit step and slope policy, and add the support platform's point velocity/displacement. It also needs an explicit policy for pushing dynamic bodies. Use Box2D's mover helpers if and only if they exist in the pin; otherwise build it from the pinned overlap and shape-cast APIs. That is a different controller contract and should be benchmarked separately.

## 4. Resolve one-way platforms before the solver

A one-way platform is a solid collision shape with a pre-solve decision, not a sensor and not a contact disabled after `b2World_Step`. Mark the small set of relevant shapes for pre-solve callbacks. For a character/platform pair, decide from stable tick state: the platform's allowed local normal/top plane, the character's previous foot position, relative normal velocity, a tolerance/hysteresis band, and an explicit drop-through timer. Disable while approaching from the forbidden side or during drop-through; once the character is accepted above the top plane, keep the contact enabled until it has clearly separated. Account for moving and rotating platforms by evaluating in platform space.

Post-step disabling is too late because impulses have already been solved. A rule based only on the current position can also flip while overlapping, so tests must cover passage from below, landing from above, side contact, jumping, drop-through, fast descent, platform upward/downward motion, reversal, spawn overlap, and stacked one-way platforms.

## 5. Define ownership, IDs, and event lifetimes

Opaque 3.x IDs are handles, not durable gameplay identities. Revision bits and debug validity checks can expose some stale uses, but they are not a lifetime system.

Use these rules:

- The world registry owns all Box2D objects. An entity has a stable game handle `(index, generation)` mapped to its current body ID. Collider and joint records have the same kind of stable handle and store their current Box2D IDs only inside the adapter.
- A body owns its attached shapes. The adapter also records every incident joint. Destruction is normalized into a tick-boundary command: remove joints, remove/clear shape records, destroy the body, clear the mapping, and increment the game generation. Even if Box2D cascades some destruction, the adapter must invalidate every corresponding record.
- Never put a raw `b2BodyId`, `b2ShapeId`, `b2JointId`, event pointer, manifold pointer, or event-array element into a later-frame queue. Translate it immediately to stable game handles and copy only required scalar event data.
- Drain body/contact/sensor event arrays immediately after each step and before any relevant object is destroyed or the next step begins. Treat the buffers as borrowed until the next step/API invalidation point specified by the pin. Use validity checks only as assertions, not as recovery.
- Defer gameplay-requested destruction until event draining and contact/support extraction finish. When an overlapped sensor or visitor is destroyed, remove its stable handle from gameplay overlap sets explicitly; do not assume a future end event.

Sensors should generate transient begin/end observations. Gameplay owns the persistent trigger-overlap set keyed by stable game handles. Contact events similarly report transitions; they are not persistent contact objects. Enable event production only on shapes that need it, because event volume is part of the budget.

## 6. Scope CCD and bullets

Do not enable bullet mode on every moving body. It increases continuous-collision work and does not replace sensible shape sizes, fixed stepping, or gameplay sweeps. First use the pinned revision's default continuous/speculative behavior and measure misses. Enable bullet behavior only for bodies whose required collision class needs the stronger sweep—for example, a small fast physical projectile that must hit moving dynamic targets. Define the threshold from displacement per substep relative to the projectile diameter and thinnest required target, then validate it with a speed/size/angle/target-motion matrix.

Hitscan weapons should ray cast. Projectiles whose gameplay only needs the first impact can often shape cast their previous-to-next pose and resolve the hit directly. Reserve simulated bullet bodies for projectiles that need physical flight, ricochet, or impulses. Compare those three implementations in the adversarial projectile suite.

## 7. State the determinism claim narrowly

A seed does not make floating-point simulation portable. A defensible initial claim is: the same pinned Box2D binary and game build, fixed tick/substeps, floating-point environment, initial creation order/state, command order, task implementation/configuration, and tick input stream reproduce the tested per-tick hashes on the tested machine/configuration.

Do not choose worker count from hardware concurrency for a rollback protocol. Freeze it initially, preferably at one while establishing the golden replay. If the pinned Box2D revision claims deterministic ordered multithreading, verify the actual task integration at worker counts 1, 2, 4, and the shipping count; only then claim worker-count invariance for that exact pin/build and tested range. Different CPU features, compilers, floating-point contraction/fast-math settings, standard libraries, operating systems, or future Box2D revisions are separate qualification targets, not implied guarantees.

Comparing only final player transforms can miss an earlier divergence in velocity, other bodies, contacts, joint state, trigger state, or game logic. Hash every tick in stable game-handle order: all rollback-relevant body transforms and velocities, awake/enabled state where exposed and relevant, object existence/generations, gameplay controller/support/trigger state, joint/game state, input and command order, and translated events. On mismatch, save the first divergent tick and a structured state diff. Box2D does not provide a general public snapshot of all solver/contact warm-start state; rebuilding from spawn records is not equivalent to restoring an arbitrary mid-simulation world. Replaying from the identical initial construction and complete command/input history may be reproducible within the narrow contract above, but a transform-only checkpoint is not sufficient.

## 8. Executable evidence plan

Run release builds after a warm-up, for enough ticks to expose tails, and preserve raw samples plus the complete build/simulation manifest.

| Suite | Required cases | Evidence / gate |
|---|---|---|
| API/lifetime | Adapter compile probe; wrong-header/link rejection; all joint/body/shape destruction orders; destroy while overlapping; world teardown | No invalid-call diagnostics, stale gameplay mappings, or queued raw IDs; sanitizers/debug validation clean |
| Clock | Render schedules at 48, 60, 90, 144, and 240 Hz; jitter; long frame; catch-up cap | Identical simulation tick/input sequence and per-tick hashes regardless of render schedule; documented overload behavior |
| Character/support | Flat/slope/wall/ceiling; seams; platform translation, rotation, acceleration, reversal, edge, sleep/wake; multiple simultaneous contacts | No false grounded ticks or duplicate land transitions; support body/normal correct; numeric penetration and drift limits pass |
| One-way | Below-to-above, above landing, side, jump, drop-through, fast fall, moving/rotating platform, spawn overlap, stacked platforms | Expected enabled/disabled decision recorded per tick; zero incorrect blocks/falls in the corpus |
| Sensors/events | Multiple overlapping actors; rapid enter/exit; sensor/body destruction; event storm | Exactly-once gameplay transitions where specified; overlap sets empty correctly; copied handles remain valid |
| Joints/lifts | Loaded lift, reversal, limit/motor cases, destruction of either endpoint, low-FPS catch-up | Explicit joint drift/overshoot limits pass; no dangling joint records |
| Projectile/CCD | Speed × radius × target thickness × impact angle × static/kinematic/dynamic target × substeps; bullet off/on; ray/shape cast alternatives | Zero misses in the declared gameplay envelope; smallest-cost CCD scope selected |
| Dense performance | About 2,000 active shapes with representative contacts, sensors, joints, sleeping/waking, platform motion, and projectile bursts; worker-count matrix | Step plus adapter p50/p95/p99/max, catch-up cost, and peak memory meet the predeclared budget with headroom |
| Replay | Repeated same-binary runs; worker matrix; Windows/Linux and compiler/CPU qualification lanes; intentional one-tick perturbation | First-divergence tick detected; only tested configurations are certified; any Box2D/build change invalidates the old certificate |

For every performance run, capture Box2D's pinned `b2World_GetProfile` and `b2World_GetCounters` output (using the exact fields available in that revision), wall-clock step time, adapter event/query time, body/shape/contact/joint/island counts, sensor/contact event counts, task count, awake count, bullet count, allocation/peak memory data, and scene seed/input trace. Report percentiles and histograms, not one average. Keep separate cold-start and steady-state results and test the shipping task scheduler on each OS.

The release gate is the fixed-rate/substep/worker configuration with the lowest measured cost that passes all correctness envelopes and remains under the percentile budget. Fail the gate on a stale API probe, any lifetime diagnostic, any replay hash divergence inside a claimed configuration, any projectile/one-way miss inside the declared envelope, or a p99 budget regression.

## Workflow boundary

Keep this Box2D adapter responsible for the pinned API manifest, ID translation/lifetimes, fixed-tick `b2World_Step` bridge, callbacks/events, character collision policy, CCD policy, Box2D profiles/counters, and the Box2D qualification corpus. Route the generic accumulator/render interpolation and overload policy to the core simulation-loop workflow. Route input logging, snapshot/checkpoint design, replay versioning, state hashing/diffing, peer compatibility, and rollback-window strategy to the core rollback/determinism workflow. Route benchmark orchestration, statistical regression gates, and CI artifact retention to the core performance workflow. The adapter supplies those workflows with deterministic tick commands, stable handles, hashes, metrics, and manifests rather than reimplementing them.

enabled.response:
## Source snapshot and drift

Box2D v3.1.1 was released on 2025-06-04 at commit 8c661469c9507d3ad6fbd2fea3f1aa71669c2fe3. The release says there was no documentation update: website Doxygen 3.1.0 remains stale, so the v3.1.1 tagged public headers are the final API authority. Current main commit 617d32ab02570930625bbcb8479f54be9bf8d045 labels 3.2.0 and contains experimental snapshot, recording, and state-hash APIs; these are outside stable 3.1.1 and must not leak into 3.1.1 code.

## IDs, ownership, and mutation

Initialize definitions with b2DefaultWorldDef, b2DefaultBodyDef, b2DefaultShapeDef, and b2DefaultChainDef. Opaque C IDs are generational and validity checks cover up to 64K allocations, so durable application IDs own identity. Destroying a world destroys its objects; destroying a body destroys attached shapes and joints; a chain owns segment shape IDs, which are invalidated with the chain. b2DestroyShape's updateBodyMass choice and b2Body_ApplyMassFromShapes define mass recompute; sensor shapes may have mass and a shape cannot start or stop being a sensor. Use no 2.4 fixtures, pointers, or contact listeners.

## Fixed step and task phase

Use fixed dt; select substeps from measured stability and cost, then freeze the substep count, with events consumed after each main step. workerCount requires enqueueTask and finishTask. b2World_Step locks the world; callbacks and worker tasks are thread-safe and perform no world mutation. Adapter policy permits no world reads during the step either, and confines read-only queries to an outside-step phase.

## Events and sensors

Body move events have no opt-in flag and are available after every step, and with sleeping disabled every dynamic and kinematic body produces move events. Sensor, contact, hit, and PreSolve shape flags default false, and drain all borrowed event arrays after every step. End touch events can contain destroyed IDs, so use b2Shape_IsValid as an invalid-access guard before API dereference, never as identity, translate/copy to stable application IDs, tombstone destroyed identities, and never queue raw elements. Sensors can detect other sensors. Engine event order is not gameplay semantic order, so canonicalize a persistent gameplay overlap set.

## Queries and tree semantics

OverlapAABB is an approximate broadphase bounding-box candidate query, and use OverlapShape or another narrow-phase exact test. Ray-cast and shape-cast callbacks arrive in arbitrary order, so collect multiple hits and sort by fraction plus durable identity. In v3.1.1, b2World_CastShape reports an initial overlap with zero fraction, zero normal, and an arbitrary point. b2World_CastRayClosest ignores initial overlap, ray casts starting inside treat the shape as a miss, and b2World_CastMover also ignores initial overlap, so use b2World_CollideMover for depenetration planes. Consume callback results immediately with no persistence.

## One-way PreSolve

Set enablePreSolveEvents and use b2PreSolveFcn before collision resolution. Contacts re-enable, so re-disable every step. The callback runs in a parallel-for/worker thread, must be thread-safe, must not read or write the world, and disabling after the step is too late. Stable v3.1.1 documents a high-speed limitation that may pause; keep the Platformer sample as a test seed and add project cases.

## Experimental character mover

The stable 3.1.1 experimental mover is a geometric capsule outside world ownership, not a body. Call b2World_CollideMover and b2World_CastMover, assemble collision planes, run b2SolvePlanes for translation, then b2ClipVector for velocity. It is not a complete controller: gameplay owns steps, slopes, persistent state, pushing, rotation, support, and replication policy.

## CCD boundary

Default CCD covers dynamic bodies versus static bodies. Bullet mode extends a sparse tested body to static, kinematic, and dynamic targets but not other bullets; use it sparingly because it may interfere with joints. Sensors have no CCD. Continuous-collision contact events can appear on the next step, so gameplay must not require same-step delivery.

## Determinism is not rollback

The official cross-platform claim is for 64-bit targets and creation-order-derived simulation/events: precise FP on MSVC, floating-point contraction disabled on Clang/GCC, tested on x64 and ARM. The pinned determinism test uses 1/60, 4 substeps, worker counts 1-5, expected sleep step 288, and hash 0x35467e1e; application determinism is still required, so this is not proof. Stable v3.1.1 has no public snapshot and no rollback support; transforms are insufficient, there is no cross-version guarantee, and only the pinned exact build plus complete replay can be qualified.

## Review verdict

Reject the current design. It combines an unstable API boundary, render-driven simulation, stale IDs, post-solve collision changes, persistent borrowed events, indiscriminate bullets, and a replay test incapable of detecting most divergence.

### Pinned adapter contract

Adapter policy:

- Vendor or fetch exactly v3.1.1 commit `8c661469c9507d3ad6fbd2fea3f1aa71669c2fe3`.
- Record the source-tree, public-header, and built-library hashes; CMake options; architecture; compiler and version; floating-point and contraction flags; worker/task configuration; and adapter version.
- Compile a small API probe against only those tagged headers and linked library. CI must reject 2.4 fixtures, pointers, listeners, C++ object APIs, iteration-pair `Step`, and experimental 3.2 symbols.
- Treat the tagged headers—not stale website documentation or copied `main` snippets—as the symbol authority.

### Tick and task policy

Run simulation from an integer tick accumulator, never directly from render delta:

```text
apply stable-sorted tick commands
precompute immutable callback context
b2World_Step(world, fixedDt, frozenSubsteps)
copy and translate all event arrays
run outside-step queries
resolve support/overlap transitions
queue next-tick mutations
compute the semantic tick hash
render interpolated state independently
```

At 48 Hz the renderer may consume one or two completed simulation ticks; at 240 Hz it may render several times between ticks. Backlog policy may skip rendering or report overload, but it must not change `fixedDt`, substeps, or worker count.

Use `1/60` as the initial measurement lane because it matches the pinned upstream determinism seed, not as an unexplained shipping constant. Test `1/60` and any gameplay-required higher tick such as `1/120`, with substeps `{1, 2, 4, 8}`. Ship the cheapest pair that passes every stability and collision gate within budget, and freeze it in the replay compatibility identity.

Do not use hardware concurrency as session configuration. Prefer one worker if it meets the budget; otherwise select one measured fixed count and require `enqueueTask`, `finishTask`, correct worker indices, bounded callback work, and stable output reduction. Different worker-count lanes may be qualified experimentally, not assumed interchangeable.

### Ownership and lifetime

Maintain mappings such as:

```text
ApplicationBodyId  <-> current b2BodyId
ApplicationShapeId <-> current b2ShapeId
ApplicationJointId <-> current b2JointId
ApplicationChainId <-> chain plus segment identities
```

Raw Box2D IDs live only inside the adapter and only while their mappings are valid. Gameplay records, event queues, rollback logs, and persistent overlap/support state contain application IDs.

Normalize creates and destroys at tick boundaries in deterministic application-ID order. On body destruction, invalidate its bodies, attached shapes, chain segments, and joints as one cascade; on world destruction, invalidate everything. Copy application identity into an event record before any later destruction, maintain tombstones for end events, and call `b2Shape_IsValid` only before dereferencing an engine ID.

Define shape mass policy explicitly. Every shape removal selects the appropriate `updateBodyMass` behavior, deferred batches end with `b2Body_ApplyMassFromShapes`, and sensor density is accounted for deliberately. Sensor status changes require shape recreation.

### Player and moving-platform contract

Use a solver-driven dynamic capsule as the production player contract. It best matches the required physical interaction with moving platforms and lifts; do not teleport it onto ray hits.

A downward ray is only an observation and must not define grounded state by itself. After each tick, classify support from all applicable foot-region contacts using acceptable support normal, side/foot location, relative separation or velocity, platform identity, and one-way eligibility. Reduce multiple candidates deterministically by durable ID, retain one support identity, and emit landing only on the unsupported-to-supported transition.

Platform-relative velocity must inform player control. A translating or rotating support must be handled as support motion, rather than repeatedly snapping the player to a query point. Test relative foot drift explicitly.

Use narrow-phase overlap or shape casts as auxiliary probes for clearance and anticipation. Sort multi-hit results; handle initial overlap separately, because `b2World_CastShape` supplies no useful initial-overlap normal. Queries never produce persistent objects.

The experimental mover is an alternative whole-controller contract, not an add-on to the dynamic capsule. If later selected, replace the body controller and explicitly implement support motion, steps, slopes, pushing, rotation, events, persistence, and replication; do not combine it with body teleportation and solver contacts.

### One-way platforms

Enable PreSolve only for shapes that need it. Before the step, publish immutable metadata keyed by durable shape identity: platform side, transform/motion facts, previous foot/support state, drop-through state, and qualification limits.

For every relevant contact and every step, `b2PreSolveFcn` decides whether the contact is enabled using:

- Approach from the solid side.
- Previous foot position/state.
- Player/platform relative velocity.
- Explicit drop-through state.
- Translating and rotating platform motion.
- Spawn-overlap handling.
- Edge/corner behavior.
- A tested maximum crossing speed.

Disabling the contact after `b2World_Step` cannot undo solved impulses. Because stable PreSolve has a documented high-speed limitation, publish a qualified speed envelope. Outside it, use a separately tested cast-based clamp or a conservative two-sided policy rather than promising one-way behavior.

### Sensors and events

Drain body, sensor, contact, and hit arrays after each main step and immediately copy the needed fields plus stable application IDs. Treat them as transient deltas.

Maintain one canonical application-owned overlap set keyed by `(sensorApplicationId, visitorApplicationId)`. Deduplicate sensor–sensor reports, sort deltas deterministically, and generate gameplay enter/exit transitions from the set. Destruction removes/tombstones identities without dereferencing invalid end-touch IDs.

If a fast object must trigger a volume within the same tick, sensors alone cannot provide that guarantee. Sweep the object with a ray or shape cast and merge the result into the gameplay trigger policy deterministically.

### CCD and projectiles

Do not enable bullet mode on every moving body. Keep ordinary moving players, platforms, and jointed lifts on their measured default policy.

Use bullet mode only for sparse projectile bodies whose declared collision envelope requires dynamic-versus-kinematic or dynamic-versus-dynamic CCD. Bullet mode does not cover bullet-versus-bullet CCD and may interfere with joints.

For each projectile class choose one measured policy:

- Physical bullet when solver response and later event delivery are acceptable.
- Ray cast for point-like or hitscan behavior.
- Shape cast for finite-radius swept impacts.
- Explicit sweep logic for fast trigger crossings or bullet-versus-bullet requirements.

Gameplay must tolerate continuous-contact events arriving on the following step, or use the cast result as the authoritative same-tick impact.

## Executable evidence plan

### 1. Artifact and API gates

For every Windows and Linux artifact:

1. Print and archive source, header, and library hashes and all build flags.
2. Compile the v3.1.1-only adapter probe.
3. Run the pinned upstream determinism test at `1/60`, four substeps, and worker counts 1–5.
4. Require sleep step `288` and hash `0x35467e1e`.
5. Reject the artifact if any recorded hash or API-domain check differs.

This proves only that the artifact matches the upstream seed.

### 2. Stability/cost selection matrix

Run the complete representative world for each candidate:

```text
fixed tick:  1/60, 1/120
substeps:    1, 2, 4, 8
workers:     1 and each proposed fixed production count
scene:       ordinary, dense 2,000-active-shape, contact-heavy worst case
duration:    warm-up plus long steady-state and burst/catch-up runs
```

Record per tick:

- Total `b2World_Step`, task, event-drain, query, and controller CPU time.
- Available Box2D phase profiles and solver counters.
- Awake bodies, shapes, islands/pairs/contacts, and joint load.
- Body, contact, hit, and sensor event counts.
- Allocation or scratch high-water marks exposed by the pinned build.
- Simulation backlog under 48, 60, 144, and 240 Hz render schedules.
- Per-tick semantic hash and first divergence.

Report p50, p95, p99, p99.9, maximum, and distributions—not one average. Require the chosen configuration to remain within the declared 3 ms policy on minimum hardware; if 3 ms is a hard ceiling, maximum time is the gate, otherwise state and enforce the accepted percentile plus backlog limit.

### 3. Character and one-way adversarial suite

Run scripted cases for:

- Landing, walking, jumping, and grazing corners.
- Multiple simultaneous contacts without duplicate land events.
- Low-render-rate and jittered-render schedules with identical tick inputs.
- Moving-platform start, stop, reversal, translation, rotation, edge departure, and platform destruction.
- One-way approach above/below, drop-through, spawn overlap, resting contact, fast crossing, thin platform, edge/corner contact, and opposing platform velocity.
- Initial query overlap and multi-hit queries returned in different orders.

Pass conditions include no grounded flicker, exactly one landing transition, no underside sticking, bounded platform-relative drift, deterministic support identity, and an explicit pass/fallback boundary for high-speed one-way crossings.

### 4. Lifetime and event suite

Fuzz deterministic create/destroy commands, including body-with-shapes-and-joints destruction, chain destruction, world teardown, event delivery adjacent to destruction, deferred mass updates, sensor recreation, sensor–sensor overlap, and more than 64K allocation churn.

Instrument every engine dereference. Require zero stale-ID dereferences, zero raw IDs in gameplay/rollback storage, complete cascade invalidation, balanced canonical overlap sets, and identical results under deliberately permuted raw callback/event order.

### 5. CCD matrix

Cross:

```text
projectile speed and radius
target thickness
impact angle
static, kinematic, dynamic, and bullet targets
stationary and moving targets
substep candidate
default CCD, bullet, ray cast, and shape cast
```

Measure missed impacts, duplicate impacts, penetration, response, joint disturbances, event latency, and CPU cost. The shipping policy must have zero misses within each declared projectile envelope; behavior outside the envelope must be documented as unsupported or routed through another sweep policy.

### 6. Replay qualification

Replay fixed tick inputs and complete ordered commands, never captured render deltas. Deterministically recreate the world, including creation order, definitions, application state, overlap/support state, RNG state, joint state inputs, destruction commands, callback reductions, and event consumption order.

Every tick, hash a durable-ID-sorted semantic projection containing all accessible bodies and relevant velocities/state, joint/gameplay state, persistent overlaps, support identity, commands, and gameplay outputs. Final player transforms are only one field.

Run:

- Repeated identical executions on each exact artifact.
- Worker counts 1–5.
- Supported Windows/Linux compiler and CPU lanes.
- Long uninterrupted runs.
- Rollbacks of varied window lengths and repeated resimulation.
- Render schedules from 48–240 Hz plus jitter and hitches.
